report.answer_text:
What it is
Suzetrigine (Journavx) is a 50 mg oral tablet. The FDA approved it on January 30, 2025, as a first-in-class non-opioid analgesic for moderate to severe acute pain in adults.[1] The approval went to Vertex Pharmaceuticals.[1] It was previously known as VX-548.
How it works
Suzetrigine blocks pain signals on their way to the brain and spinal cord. It does this by selectively inhibiting NaV1.8 voltage-gated sodium channels.[2] These channels are part of a pain-signaling pathway in the peripheral nervous system, so the drug acts before pain signals reach the brain.[1]
Why it was notable
A new drug class. Vertex described it as the first new class of pain medicine approved in more than 20 years.[3]
A non-opioid option. It offers an alternative to opioids for acute pain. The FDA's acting CDER director said a non-opioid pain reliever offers a chance to mitigate certain risks of opioid use.[4] No opioid-type dependence was seen in clinical trials.[5]
Regulatory support. The application received Breakthrough Therapy, Fast Track and Priority Review designations.[1]
Evidence behind it
Approval rested on two phase 3 randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials, one after abdominoplasty and one after bunionectomy.[2] Both showed a statistically significant greater reduction in pain than placebo.[1] Suzetrigine eased pain about as effectively as Vicodin (hydrocodone/acetaminophen), according to Yale Medicine.[6] One caveat is that it was compared with Vicodin rather than stronger opioids like oxycodone or morphine.[6]
Safety notes
Common side effects were itching, muscle spasms, increased creatine phosphokinase, and rash.[1]
It is contraindicated with strong CYP3A inhibitors, and patients should avoid grapefruit.[1]
It is not known whether it is safe and effective in children.[3]
It is approved only for acute pain, not chronic pain. Real-world studies are still needed to assess its relative effectiveness and long-term safety.[7]
